King: Movie of the week? Spelling: Right. Movie of the weeks. King: When did you know she had cancer? Spelling: I found out about a year -- when I first heard, I don't know if it was a year or two years ago when we first heard, and I contacted her. I hadn't talked to her in a while. (CNN) — Farrah Fawcett, the actress known around the world for her beauty and her iconic role on “Charlie’s Angels,” is reportedly gravely ill and may be nearing death after a long battle with cancer.

Fawcett, shown here in 2004, is the subject of a documentary chronicling her fight with the disease. The documentary, airing Friday night on NBC, offers an intimate look at her life since her diagnosis.

On Thursday, Larry King spoke with Candy Spelling, a close friend of Fawcett. Spelling’s late husband, Aaron Spelling, produced “Charlie’s Angels.” In the interview, Spelling discussed her relationship with Fawcett and why she believes the actress chose to participate in the documentary.

The following is an edited version of the interview.

**Larry King:** Did you first meet Farrah in connection with her getting that part?

**Candy Spelling:** Yes. Actually, she did a lot of small parts in movies for Aaron starting around 1973. So it’s been, my God, 36 or 37 years since I first met her.

*Watch Candy Spelling talk about her friendship with Farrah Fawcett »*

**King:** So you knew her well during all that time?

**Spelling:** Yes.

**King:** Did you know about her being chosen for “Charlie’s Angels”?

**Spelling:** I remember. She did some small roles. I think the one that made Aaron decide he was really going to use her was this American beauty pageant and also something like “Murder on Flight 502.” He did the 90-minute versions.

**King:** Movie of the week?

**Spelling:** Right. Movies of the week.

**King:** When did you learn she had cancer?

**Spelling:** I found out about a year — when I first heard, I don’t know if it was a year or two years ago — and I contacted her. I hadn’t talked to her in a while. She said, “I’m going to be all right, Candy. Everything is going to be all right.”

**King:** Why do you think, Candy, she agreed to do the documentary?

**Spelling:** I think she wanted to give courage to other people who are fighting this kind of thing. I know how devastating the press was when Aaron had cancer. It’s just so difficult. It’s hard to have a private life at that point.

**King:** Why do the tabloids become so harsh toward someone in such pain?

**Spelling:** It’s news. It’s a sad thing. I’m always so sorry to see it. But people believe what they see, and a lot of times, we don’t know how true it really is.

(CNN) — Farrah Fawcett, the actress celebrated internationally for her looks and for starring in “Charlie’s Angels,” is said to be gravely ill and possibly nearing the end of her life following a lengthy struggle with cancer.

Fawcett, shown in a 2004 photo, is the subject of a documentary about her cancer battle. The program, scheduled to air Friday night on NBC, offers a personal view of her life after her diagnosis.

On Thursday, Larry King spoke with Candy Spelling, a close friend of Fawcett’s. Spelling’s late husband, Aaron Spelling, was the producer of “Charlie’s Angels.” In the interview, Candy Spelling discussed her friendship with Fawcett and explained why she thinks Fawcett agreed to make the documentary.

What follows is an edited transcript of their conversation.

**Larry King:** Did you originally meet Farrah because she was being considered for that role?

**Candy Spelling:** Yes. In fact, beginning around 1973, she appeared in a number of small film roles for Aaron. So, my goodness, it has been about 36 or 37 years since I first met her.

**King:** So you were well acquainted with her throughout that whole period?

**Spelling:** Yes.

**King:** Were you aware when she was chosen for “Charlie’s Angels”?

**Spelling:** I remember it. She had been doing smaller parts. I think the project that really convinced Aaron he wanted to use her was an American beauty pageant, and also something like “Murder on Flight 502.” He was making the 90-minute programs then.

**King:** The movie-of-the-week format?

**Spelling:** Exactly. Movies of the week.

**King:** When did you learn that she had cancer?

**Spelling:** I heard about it roughly a year ago — or maybe it was two years ago when we first learned about it — and I reached out to her. We hadn’t spoken in some time. She told me, “I’m going to be all right, Candy. Everything is going to be all right.”

**King:** Candy, why do you believe she chose to make the documentary?

**Spelling:** I think she wanted to encourage other people who are battling the same kind of illness. I know how devastating the media coverage was when Aaron had cancer. It is just incredibly hard. At that stage, it becomes very difficult to have any privacy.

**King:** Why are the tabloids so harsh toward someone who is suffering so much?

**Spelling:** Because it’s considered news. It’s very sad, and I’m always sorry to see it happen. But people often accept what they read or see, even though many times we don’t really know how accurate it is.
